questions.q: What are the two ways to write a cast in PySpark?
options: A string type name like "int", or a type class like IntegerType() imported from pyspark.sql.types
Only a string type name works — type classes cannot be used for casting
You must always write a full StructType just to cast one column
Casting requires a separate SparkSession configuration setting
questions.explain: Both forms do the same thing — the type-class form uses the same module Lesson 43 used for schemas.

questions.q: What happens when .cast() is applied to a value that can't actually convert, like the text "N/A" being cast to double?
options: The value becomes null for that row — not an error, and the job keeps running
PySpark immediately throws an exception and stops the entire job
The value is automatically converted to zero
The entire row is silently deleted from the DataFrame
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 47's when()/otherwise() behavior — PySpark tends to turn 'doesn't fit' into null rather than crash.

questions.q: Why is a silent cast failure a real risk in production pipelines?
options: Because bad or malformed data can hide as null values without raising any error at all, going undetected
It isn't a risk — casts always succeed with real-world data
Because it slows down the pipeline dramatically every time
Because it always corrupts every other column in the DataFrame
questions.explain: Lesson 51 (Null Handling) is exactly where a pipeline would catch and address nulls like these.

questions.q: How does inferSchema=True from Lesson 40 relate to .cast()?
options: inferSchema performs the same kind of type-guessing/casting automatically behind the scenes, rather than by hand on one column
They are completely unrelated operations with nothing in common
inferSchema disables all casting for the rest of the DataFrame's life
.cast() can only be used on DataFrames that were read with inferSchema=True
questions.explain: An explicit schema (Lesson 43) does the same thing up front instead of guessed; .cast() does it by hand, after the fact.

questions.q: Why does CSV data especially need type casting?
options: CSV has no real types at all — everything is text until something casts it, whether automatically (inferSchema) or by hand
CSV files always store data pre-typed in binary form
Casting is only needed for JSON files, never CSV
CSV automatically converts every column to the correct type on read
questions.explain: This is the same underlying gap that both inferSchema and explicit schemas exist to address.
